utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Before we have the witness, I believe that we will hear the response from the Defence concerning of the response filed by the Prosecution to the Defence motion concerning tendering of the military expert report. And the Prosecution filed this motion the day before yesterday, and it says "Having again reviewed the report in the light of the Defence objection, the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber that it no longer intends to rely upon the report in its entirety or in an abridged form. The Prosecution seeks a general opinion from the General as to the duty and humanitarian law of a superior and, in particular, the practical steps that a superior should take when he or she has received actual inquiry notice of the criminality of his or her subordinates." The Prosecution further claimed that "The Trial Chamber, of course, retains its role in deciding whether to accept the expert's view point and deciding the weight to be given to it." So at this moment, since this witness is supposed to be here sometime next week, we would like to hear the initial response from the Defence. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The initial response is that we oppose any such last-minute attempt to change the Prosecution case. We've got opposition based in -- on substantial objections and we've got procedural objections which are not mere procedural objections but procedural objections that go to preserve the fairness of the trial and the safety of it. In the first place, in terms of substantial objections, we note that what is clearly being sought here is an attempt to create obligations where the Prosecution are unable to identify what they are at the moment. In this report here, you're not told what the Prosecution are going to say about the obligations Mr. Halilovic had. The Prosecution themselves still don't know. They are going to see him tomorrow. And Mr. Re made the point here in Court that the law about this is very scant, I think was his word, or very thin, and the substantive objection, therefore, is that -- or one of the substantive objections is this: The Prosecution doesn't know what the law is. They say Mr. Halilovic should have known what the law is. They say he should have complied with something that they don't know what it is. They are going to find out on Friday what a British general who has no law degree says it is today in 2005. Now, that is -- offends against a number of principles. It is an ultimate issue question, firstly. Secondly, it clearly steps into Your Honour's function. You, the Bench, are the experts in international humanitarian law and it is you who will decide these matters, and you will not be assisted by a non-lawyer making general comments about international humanitarian law. It's just not his field of expertise. Mr. Re indicated what a good CV this person had, and as a military expert speaking about his area of expertise he has very impressive qualifications. But that's not what is being asked of him. He's being asked, it's quite clear, to give general -- a general opinion, I'm not making this up myself but quoting from Mr. Re's -- "a general opinion from the general as to the duties under international humanitarian law of a superior and in particular the practical steps that he should take." Now Your Honours are familiar with what is in here; I won't read it back. It's quite clear what is being sought here is in effect a judgement, a ruling of law. The Prosecutor says you retain your role in deciding whether to accept that or not, but of course you do. But that applies to the Prosecution's closing submissions. And what's really being sought here is to get into evidence the Prosecution's closing submission, to say, Look, Halilovic should have done this, this is what international humanitarian law requires and Halilovic should have complied with it. But they don't know what international humanitarian law required. They've made that absolutely clear. This document here is -- I mean, I feel like tender this in evidence myself because it makes it quite clear that -- well, it's one aspect of their case only, of course. There are many other parts that remain in contention, but on this aspect the Prosecution doesn't know what the requirements were, nor do they put before the Court any coherent version of what was required. And this therefore, is not a proper area for expertise and it's not a proper area for expert opinion so we are against it on that basis. We are against it on another of other bases as well. Apart from the ultimate issue objection, the invading in the Trial Chamber's area of discretion objection, the procedural objections here are not mere procedure. It is an astounding situation in this, a Tribunal of this level of law, that at the end of a case like this, we have expended our energies on dealing with it this witness, and frankly with a view to discrediting him to be told now, Well, that's not the evidence he's going to give. You've wasted your time. Now we are going to call something completely different from him, general legal evidence about what international human -- humanitarian law requires. And we don't know what he's going to say. They haven't given us the report. They are going to see him on Friday. I spoke to Mr. Re and he indicated to me, and I'm -- we are grateful to him, of course, for trying the best that he can and we are not making a personal criticism of Mr. Re. He's got a case to deal with, he's got to try to put it as well as he can to the Court. So what I'm saying now is not meant to be a personal criticism. He's going to go to London, he's going to endeavour to get a report of some description from the general and then he's going to endeavour to provide that to us electronically as soon as he can. So if the Prosecution -- if things go well for them, they may be in a position to provide us with a document on Friday. Now, these events happened in 1993. The investigation was on foot by 1996, as you've heard from this witness, and the trial itself has been on foot for a long time. I suppose I'm beating the obvious now to say it's too late. You can't introduce evidence like this when it's suspicious -- well, it's -- I say suspicious when it's -- when a -- on a -- on a substantive basis whatever this witness says, bearing in mind what the Prosecution say they want from him, whatever he says is likely to be inadmissible and not useful because it -- for the substantive reasons I've said. The Defence is -- we are not on notice yet what he's going to say. We don't know what he's going to say. We can't get expert opinions of our own of what he's going to say. We can do the best we can. We have been in the case, of course, and we know the evidence and we are with some fortunate expertise in international humanitarian on our team. But this is not a way to run a trial. You don't come at the end of the trial and say you can have four, maybe five days notice to deal with a whole new area of law a general opinion on international humanitarian law. And for those reasons you should enforce the rules -- I'm sorry, my learned -- I just didn't know my learned friend was coming, actually. He's here. Your Honours I'm happy just so that Mr. Re can understand what's being said here, and I'd better -- I'll recapitulate very briefly. I won't repeat it all but -- just so he understands it, that we are saying that there are substantive objections and procedural objections. The substantive ones are an as indicated, it's an invasion of the Trial Chamber's duties and it breaches the ultimate issue rule. It won't assist the Tribunal. It will waste your time. In fact, it's not a proper area nor expertise, nor does this witness have the expertise to give that evidence, and I'm now moving on to the procedural matters. The procedural matters in short are that we don't have the report, we are not going to be able to prepare for it properly, it's doubtful that we would -- this is not something that will be cured by adjournment. I mean, we have other things we have to do now and we are becoming busy. We've got a 98 bis to consider. We've got a Defence case to consider for what remains of the case, if any, after the 98 bis stage and we also have, of course, to -- to deal with two witnesses. And this witness now who has come up with a with a major new amount of evidence that Your Honours have seen. And you'll assess that as you wish in the future but I have to deal with it and -- obviously, and that will become apparent this morning. We've been working very hard on seeking to rebut some of the -- these new allegation that have surfaced. So we are busy. We don't want this to emerge and -- now the procedural objections are that we haven't got the report, the Prosecution's failed to abide by the deadline set by the Pre-Trial Judge to disclose that report which was two years ago. And in any event, Your Honours will recall before the break, and there was an enforced break in these proceedings because Your Honours had to deal with another case, that before that break, it was discussed that by providing the expert report to us before that break, that break would not be a waste. And in fact in the course of that break we would all benefit because the Defence would have time to prepare the expert, we wouldn't need extra time et cetera, et cetera, but that hasn't happened and we are now prejudiced. So the Defence doesn't have adequate time to prepare, and nor is an adjournment going to cure that because the rest of the case is now pending. There are various pressures on this Court to finish, which we understand; we all have to finish it. And frankly, there is another thing which may not weigh strictly but it's something you've always got to consider. Mr. Halilovic is in custody here and adjournments generally are not a basis for releasing somebody from custody. Is he to sit there in custody playing volleyball with the other people out there while we consider the new report of the Prosecutor? It just shows a disregard, really, for Mr. Halilovic, frankly. Although it's not a basis that you'll decide this on, it's a relevant matter to consider, frankly. Your Honours, we are entitled to know in detail the nature of the charges against us. For a long time now, Mr. Mettraux has been asking in court what's the body of law that the Prosecutors are relying on, and now you can see why we don't get an answer. They don't know. They are not sure and they are going to go and ask General Ridgeway to give them a body of law to rely upon and then maybe they will call the witness to say how Sefer Halilovic might have been known about that. Your Honours, finally the Defence will suffer prejudice about there because whatever comes in that report surely we should have known about it so we could seek to rebut it through the actual evidence of witnesses. If, for example, witnesses such as use Jusuf Jasarevic or Vahid Karavelic are people who weren't called strictly as experts but they were people who had knowledge of particular areas. Jasarevic, Eminovic, Dzankovic were all members of the SVB. And had we known that something like this was coming perhaps -- and if we had details of what the duties that a British general thinks should have been followed, well, we might have asked the witnesses whether that duty was a practical reality in Bosnia in 1993 and we might have got answers one way or the other. We don't know, I'm pretty sure I know what the answers would be. But we can't do that now. They are gone. And we didn't have in our hands this expert report, so it will be a very platonic report in the atmosphere without any application here. Therefore it won't assist you. Sorry, Your Honour, just excuse me. Pardon me. It's pointed out that the Prosecution in fact took a decision not to call Bahrudin Camal [phoen] which, as you'll recall he was the alleged military Prosecutor available at the time to whom Halilovic should have turned and as it turned out the Prosecutors decided not to call him. Anyway, that's a peripheral matter, really, so matters of substance say that he's not a good witness and matters of form say that it's too late to try him. So we are going to oppose him. And in the event -- and, frankly, we think that it wouldn't change things if -- if we got the report here so that's why we are prepared to reply now. But I should note at this stage we are just in a difficult position because we don't have the report but Mr. Re has been good enough -- and I should indicate that we are grateful to him for taking the trouble to spell out what's intended because it means we can put an argument today and we appreciate that professional approach. But nevertheless, that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, since Mr. Re is present in this courtroom, do you want to give a short response to the Defence position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can. Thank you, Your Honours for the opportunity to address you on that. Our response, filed on the 18th, provided the day before, makes it quite clear that we no longer seek to rely upon the original report which was filed. We have taken on board the matters which Defence counsel have pointed out and also Your Honours concerns in relation to the expert commenting on the factual matters in the case. The Prosecution still says that the Trial Chamber would benefit from a very short, a very brief expert view as to the practical measures that a commander or superior could or should take in a factual situation. The Defence have always been on notice that we intended to call the expert evidence at the end of the case and that anything an expert said would be in light of the evidence given at trial. Now, the particular area of law which -- international humanitarian law in which the Trial Chamber would be greatly benefited by expert military opinion is in relation to the failure to prevent which only pertains to the charge in relation to Grabovica. As we pointed out in our motion, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and indeed under customary law is fairly thin on the ground in relation to the practical measures that a commander should take to prevent criminality. The closest we can find as we've noted in the motion is in the Blaskic -- is a combination of the Blaskic Trial Chamber judgement and the Celebici Appeals Chamber judgement. Now, they're more -- they don't go into detail as to what a commander could do or should do to prevent criminality by his subordinates. That's an area in which it's not really in our submission an area which the law particularly solves. Because it's not one you'll find in the regulations or the military -- or military hand books. It's something which comes from a combination of experience and the application of those particular rules. So that's -- that's the main area in which we would seek to bring a brief opinion on that. Now, I've spoken to my learned friend about -- I do -- we do understand it's -- where we are in the proceedings. Our intention is to have something by tomorrow, setting out what the general's opinion is on this particular matter. Now, if the Defence can't meet it when we have the report, in my respectful submission, the time to deal with it is then. If we produce something tomorrow, hand it to the Defence, and they can't deal with it in the time in our submission they can renew -- they should renew the application but they should await to see what the general has to say because it could well be something that assists the Defence. One never knows. And if the Defence asks for a ruling now instead of awaiting tomorrow, it could well, of course, prejudice the Defence preparations for their own case. We have made it quite clear that we are not seeking the expert to give any opinion on the ultimate issue or the guilt or innocence of the accused but only the theoretical position under international humanitarian law to provide the Trial Chamber with some guidance because at the end of the case, of course, it's a matter of submission by both parties based upon the -- based upon the evidence before the Trial Chamber. In our submission, the expert -- the Trial Chamber would be greatly assisted by a small piece of expert evidence which could -- we say could fill in a potential gap in the body of -- or guide the Tribunal in assisting to fill in a gap in which -- which may exist in international humanitarian law at the moment. My learned colleague also referred to the question his co-counsel, Mr. Mettraux keeps asking about the body of law. General Ridgeway isn't going to assist the Trial Chamber in the body of law which is to be applied because the body of law to be applied is clearly set out in the statute, the laws and customs of war, the Geneva Conventions, and so on. The general can only give his opinion based upon his understanding of the body of law and from his experience as the former director general of education and training in the British army and his experience in the Balkans of law, as he understand it, and the duties and what a commander could and should do under that situation. Our position is wait until they get the report tomorrow. If it can't be dealt with, then renew the application and we will review our attitude to whether we wish to pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I ask how soon we could receive that report from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The soonest would be tomorrow afternoon. We plan to speak to General Ridgeway in the morning so that the practical soonest we could get it to anyone would be tomorrow afternoon sometime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that the bench have to elaborate on that issue based on the submissions from the both parties, so right now we are not in the position to make a ruling at this moment. But, however, we will do that as early as possible. Yes. Having said that, could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Delalic. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P290?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, we may have a technical problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, what I'm hoping you have on your screen there is the letter by Mr. Karavelic dated the 5th of September. Is that what you have?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me, I apologise for the delay here. Okay. Now, here we have a letter addressed by Mr. Karavelic to Sefer Halilovic. You see there that it says that at 2200 hours last night on the night of the 4th going into the early morning of the 5th of September, that a company of soldiers from your motorised brigade was ready for the task in question. Now, that's true, that was the fact, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit from the 9th Motorised Brigade was ready but they didn't leave because of bad weather. But I don't know how it came about that this letter was drafted and why they didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just putting the facts to you at the moment. All organisational and material preparations for those units had been completed. And that's true as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember the preparations, but the unit from the 9th Motorised Brigade was supposed to leave on the 3rd but this was postponed like I said before because of Mr. Karavelic who was in disagreement with Mr. Sefer Halilovic and did not respect that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At 2230 hours, when the vehicles arrived, due to a major storm, Caco and Celo personally proposed to me, Karavelic, that the departure be postponed for 24 hours. Now, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No? And then after that, it says, "however, after that in the course of today, it was put off completely." Now that's true as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you see there that are there is a comment from Mr. Karavelic, "I am aware of the overall situation in our area in the zone of the 4th and 6th Corpses. Unfortunately such are the circumstances." Now is it your allegation that despite this letter here, that it was Vahid Karavelic himself who countermanded Sefer Halilovic's order?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking or what Mr. Karavelic was thinking. I don't know whether this was something that was countermanded or not, but I think that this pretext about the bad weather was not true. The order said that we were supposed to leave on the 3rd or the 4th. This order was not respected. Later we got another order saying that we were supposed to leave on the 6th or the 7th and we did carry out that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, the position is this: That unit was supposed to leave earlier, you say on the 3rd, and in any event according to that on the 4th. But that unit didn't go. Now, what I'm asking you is this: You had according to you a verbal order from Halilovic and an order from Karavelic, both, to send the units out and the question I'm asking you is why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade respected any order in relation to the 1st Corps and it would have respected this one as well but if it states that because of the weather it could not leave, maybe it was true, I don't really remember. I don't remember this order or an order of this type, and I think that for all of that time, there were many disagreements between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Karavelic. Mr. Karavelic thought that units should not leave Sarajevo at all to go to the Jablanica sector because he felt that the lines in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo would be weakened while Mr. Halilovic was in favour of these units leaving, and this was actually the cause of a conflict between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But never mind the conflict between them. I'm asking about you. Why didn't you send the troops out? Was it because Karavelic told you not to or was it for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I don't recall this order. I don't know. I don't know what -- how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me put a proposition to you. Is the real reason that they didn't go is simply because you and Caco decided you didn't want to go? Is that the real reason?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You make a climb don't you that later on, on or about the 7th of September that Vahid Karavelic gave you an order, an oral order, verbal order, to go out with those troops and take them to Bradina. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received such an order, the 9th Motorised Brigade did. I don't know what order the other units received but the 9th Motorised Brigade received an order on the 6th to carry out all preparations so that a unit could be sent to the Jablanica sector or actually the Bradina sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But you haven't answered my question. You received -- you, Ramiz Delalic, received an order according to you from Vahid Karavelic to take the troops to Bradina. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive an order to take the unit to Bradina myself. This was an order for the 9th Motorised Brigade to be delivered to Ramiz Delalic. But the substance of the order was not that I personally should take the unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well didn't you say -- I just want to be clear about this. Wasn't it your evidence -- wasn't it your evidence when you gave evidence on the first day here that you were told verbally by Karavelic to go out through the tunnel and to take these units as far as Bradina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true. The unit left Sarajevo at approximately -- I don't know exactly what time it was. It was dark. Because of the shelling we were waiting until it got dark so that the unit could leave Sarajevo. The unit went by itself and it reached Hrasnica. After the problems that happened in Hrasnica I received an oral order to leave in order to deal with these problems relating to the transport of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well at all events you agree with this: You claim that Karavelic sent you through the tunnel on that night, is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Got a problem here because he says, this is page 13 on the 20th of April, Your Honours, he says he didn't give any such permission for you to go through so do you stand by this, that Karavelic told you to go through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, after sending the unit off in front of the 9th Brigade command remained there for another hour to an hour and a half. We were already at the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade when we learned about the problems the units that had left Sarajevo were encountering in Hrasnica and that is when I received an oral order from Mr. Karavelic to leave Sarajevo and go there in order to resolve these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you make a claim that the commander of the 1st Corps sent people to dig trenches, in this Court?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim that it was the corps commander but there were such instances when the corps commander or his deputy would send certain individuals to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: By that corps commander are you talking about Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst others, yes, Vahid Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on Karavelic right now. You are making a claim that Karavelic sent people to dig trenches; is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not happen very often. I, for example, know of one or two cases where the commander personally sent some people to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just one second. Well, can I put this to you? It's your tactic, isn't it, to smear those who can hurt you and that's why you make this comment about Karavelic taking people to dig trenches. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did you make a claim in court on Tuesday that Sefer Halilovic sent people to dig trenches and including asking you to send people to dig trenches? Did you make that claim?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You referred to a person called Esad Cesko, didn't you, as a person taken by Halilovic -- I'm sorry, sent by you to dig trenches on the orders of Halilovic and that he had to be taken to hospital after seven days and after that he was taken away by Saco's soldiers and spent more time on the front line. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we've made an inquiry with Mr. Cesko, and I want to put this to you and ask for your response to it. Sarajevo, dated 29 April 2005. "Responding to the questions of Peter Morrissey, counsel for Sefer Halilovic" -- perhaps I'm going to circulate these. Can just ask that copies of these be given to the Judges and the Prosecutor? Your Honours I'm just going to -- because this is not uploaded I'm going to provide a hard copy to the Prosecutors and to Your Honours and there is a B/C/S version to be given to the -- to Mr. Halilovic. If you need to see a copy of this letter, you may feel free to ask for one. In fact, I think the witness should be shown a copy in B/C/S. Could he please be shown a copy in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is Mr. Cesko going to be called as a witness by the Defence. It's important for us to know this at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The answer to -- to that is, we'll see what this witness says when we he's confronted with it. Now, could the witness please be shown a copy -- he doesn't have the B/C/S yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now I just want to put this to you. You can read it. "Responding to the questions of Peter Morrissey, counsel for Sefer Halilovic before The Hague Tribunal, I can state the following." In paragraph 1 he gives some personal details which we needn't trouble you with. Then paragraph 2: "On the 1st of September 1993 three armed men unknown to me came to my business area of my company, a pastry in the Djure Djakovic street number 2, Centar municipality, and ordered me that I have to go with them to Celo's command. I objected and did not want to go. I said I will only go if I received a written request and that I will then come in myself. They went away and came back a half an hour later with a written invitation for me to report to Trampina street number 14. On the invitation it was stated that it was sent from the municipal secretariat for the People's Defence for the Centar municipality. It was signed by Armor Konjuhodzic [phoen], assistant secretary of the Centar municipality. When I arrived to the 9th Brigade -- when I arrived to the command of the 9th Brigade, a certain Dzin asked me to pay 5.000 deutschmarks in order for me to be released. I refused and said that I had I have no money, that I have already assisted the army giving my means to the 1st Corps. Dzin showed me a whole notebook of certificates with amounts on them. As I still did not want to pay, Dzin took me to Celo who I didn't know from before. Celo said I would have to go to dig trenches. They took my personal documents and clothes and they had given me a blue working suit and then they took me to the Spicasta Stijena, pointy rock, to dig trenches. I fled after a few days when I found out that Celo had left the city. I reported this case to the police administration and the military security. I stress that I had met Sefer Halilovic on a few occasions during the war and after the war. Our relationships always used to be and still are correct and we never had any disagreements. Signed Esad Cesko." Now, Mr. Delalic, what I want to put to you is Mr. Cesko was not taken the way you say on the orders of Halilovic but he was taken in the way he says on the orders of you. Do you agree with that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, the information that I have, Madam Dika who was the chief of cabinet of Sefer Halilovic as well as his lover, she told Sefer Halilovic and also she told me personally that that man should be taken for digging. So Mr. Sefer Halilovic and Dika, who was the chief of cabinet of Mr. Halilovic, they told me that that man should be sent for digging. I don't know. As far as I know, these 5.000 German marks, I don't know about that. You have to call Mr. Dzin, that is Jukic Izet who was the deputy commander for logistics in the 9th Motorised Brigade. You have to call him and ask him whether he was asking for money or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jukic is a friend of yours, isn't it, Dzin, he's a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic is a businessman from Sarajevo and he's an acquaintance of mine from the war. I know him. I haven't seen him for a while. We are not really seeing each other regularly but we know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Your claim that Sefer Halilovic sent people to take -- to dig trenches is simply an attempt by you to make him seem as bad as you, isn't that correct? Smear him.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were scores of cases in Sarajevo when Mr. Sefer Halilovic had sent people for digging or instructed that cars be seized from them. These are not just my experiences. These experiences are known to other commanders as well, and you can call them and ask them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we've also contacted Ms. Sadika Omerbegovic. I'm going to put what she's written to us as well. Perhaps if the same thing could occur here, if the English translations would be circulated to the various people. And could a Bosnian copy be provided to the accused man and also to the witness? In the meantime, I would ask that Mr. Delalic please return the copy of the previous letter that he was provided with. So the person you've referred to as Dika, her real name is Sadika Omerbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Although you're prepared to ask for private session in relation to certain matters you're prepared to simply make accusations that Sadika Omerbegovic was Halilovic's lover in open court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of Sarajevo knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Come to the substance of this letter here. "At the question of Mr. Peter Morrissey, Defence counsel representing Sefer Halilovic before The Hague Tribunal, on the circumstances of, one, giving money to Ramiz Delalic, Celo and, two, giving to Ramiz Delalic Celo a list of names of people to be taken to dig trenches, I have the following to state." We will come to paragraph 2 first of all. The other one relates to this giving of money which we'll deal with in a minute, but number 2 "in relation to the giving of names for the digging of trenches to Mr. Ramiz Delalic, this is the first time I hear something like that and while I was working in the office of the chief, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, I did not know about such information. Therefore, I state that I had never had any contacts in relation to this matter with Mr. Ramiz Delalic, nor could I have given any kind of lists for the taking of people to dig trenches. The relation with Mr. Ramiz Delalic was strictly professional and while he was the commander of the brigade he had visited the office only on a few occasions just as other commanders." Now, what's put in that paragraph that I've just read out to you that's the real truth, isn't it, Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear you. Could you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And once again, I suggest to you that you are simply here to smear Sefer Halilovic as much as you can. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody in Sarajevo knew about the relationship between Sefer Halilovic and Ms. Dika. He was really in love with her. He spent most of the time in the office and so did she at the premises where Mr. Sefer Halilovic stayed. Many people know that Mrs. Dika practically had a habit of ordering the military police and other organs to take certain individuals to dig trenches. This is not something that I have made up. All you need to do is ask around in Sarajevo and you will see whether I'm right or not. I would also like to point out that there are receipts for the money which I received or which I took. So you can also check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll come to the money in just a minute. But the fact is -- I've asked you that question already. Dealing with the money, the truth is that you were sometimes given money by the Chief of Staff in an official way with receipts given to buy weapons, is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that Sefer Halilovic had the power to give out such money because at the time he was in charge -- he was the number one person in the army and that was within his competence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: See, there has been a lot of evidence in this Court about how the troops were armed. It's the fact that you had to go sometimes and procure weapons from sources because Sarajevo was under an arms embargo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor show you any of those covert SDB sort of documents containing gossip and various claims that you were racketing business owners in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that document. On the 26th of October 1993, I was arrested, I spent seven and a half months in detention, and I was not charged or convicted for any of those cases. I am saying that all of that, all of those things are just fabrications, that all of those things were fabricated and they are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's nice to know we agree about something, Mr. Delalic because I'm putting that to you specifically that you used the money -- first of all you gathered the money generally on a voluntary basis and in a perfectly proper way, not for your own gain but to arm your soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I wasn't the one who was collecting the money. The order to collect the money was issued by the commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade, Imsirevic and the order was implemented by Jukic, Izet, and there are receipts given to the persons who voluntarily came to the brigade and gave the money. I don't know what they stated but this action was carried out by the 9th Motorised Brigade and not by Ramiz Delalic, as you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, don't misunderstand me. I'm not saying that you went around and collected the money. What I'm putting to you is this: That generally speaking any suggestion that you were racketing in weapons at that time is an absolute load of nonsense, isn't it? You were just trying to arm your troops.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there was an arms embargo. It's true that I was trying in any -- every possible way, just as all the other brigades were trying, to get in touch with some commanders who, amongst the Serbs, Chetnik commanders or amongst the Croats, with whom we could find some kind of connection in order to purchase weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Very well, thank you. Now I want to move to your departure out to Hrasnica. It's the fact, isn't it, that when you went out to Hrasnica, according to you -- I've already asked you some questions about Mr. Karavelic but I've got another one. Is it your claim that Karavelic murdered or had a hand in the murder of Caco, or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that but you can check that. You can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Have you made that claim in the past, that he was involved in the murder?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't recall ever stating anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, let's move to Hrasnica and your departure. Before we get to Hrasnica, let's just go to the lineup. On the 7th of September the troops why lined up outside your base and they were addressed by Vahid Karavelic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And these troops were the 50 or so that departed were selected from about 100, perhaps a little bit more than 100 who were originally lined up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the individual people who were there lined up were effectively chosen at the battalion level, and certainly lower than the level at which you operated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chosen at the level of the company, a company numbers about 50 men, and that is not at my level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's right. So you did not participate in the individual person-by-person selection of the troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And furthermore, although you were present with Mr. Karavelic, you didn't personally know all of the people who set off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know personally quite a number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in fact, you had at that time almost 5.000 individuals in the brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But despite various attacks that have been made on the 9th Brigade by various sources over time, the truth is most of your soldiers were good people, correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you've indicated already that it was a multi-ethnic unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And is it the fact that in the days before the war, both you and others that you knew regarded and were proud of the multi-ethnic nature of Sarajevo and the ability of the people who lived there to get on well together and cooperate properly together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you don't hate Croats yourself in any way, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you tolerate bigoted behaviour within your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I think you indicated you had almost a hundred -- I understand you weren't giving a precise figure, but you had about a hundred people of Serbian background in your unit who fought alongside the Bosniaks and Croats and other people there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand the numbers may not be perfect but -- and it would happen that troops under your command would be killed by shells fired from the Serbian positions, on a reasonably frequent basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it's a question leading to something else and it's a pretty basic one. You had people in your brigade killed by Serbs on the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, at the defence line of Sarajevo, people were shelled and killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in fact, to go a little bit further than that, it wasn't just the defence line was it? It was within the city itself that civilians were hit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But despite deaths at the hands of the Republika Srpska artillery or snipers or soldiers, you managed to preserve within your unit a tolerance and friendship between the Bosniak, Croat and Serbian soldiers who were loyal to the Bosnian government; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that it was possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And even among the troops who went down to Herzegovina, was there a soldier there - you may remember his name you may not - but a Serbian soldier named Predrag Galic, among those who departed? He was nicknamed Pedja.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember but it's possible that that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I understand what you say about all of that. And as those soldiers were selected, you saw no need, because there was no need, to point out to Karavelic, don't take those guys, they are bad guys; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say to anyone don't pick this one, don't pick that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you saw no need to do any such thing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And of course, if you had have noticed any of them to be drunk or affected by narcotic drugs, well, you would have told that to Karavelic and said don't take that bloke; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the unit was lined up, nobody was drunk or under the influence of drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I think you indicated -- well, doesn't matter what you indicated. I'll ask the question straight out. Is it the fact that you did everything you could to minimise drunken or drug-affected behaviour in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I banned alcohol and narcotics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And even though, of course, soldiers would sometimes drink alcohol when they had the opportunity, you didn't have the position that these soldiers going down to Herzegovina were a bunch of drunkards, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, of the soldiers selected by Mr. Karavelic, you didn't see any people in there who you thought, "That man has an alcohol problem." Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, most of the soldiers in Sarajevo, when they got their hands on alcohol, would definitely use it. You know very well what went on in Sarajevo. You know that Sarajevo was surrounded for more than a year, was under complete siege, so that in 90 per cent of the cases, soldiers not only from the 9th Motorised Brigade but any other brigade, if they got their hands on any alcohol would use it. So that's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand and I suppose my point really is this: Your soldiers were just normal -- could I just ask you this. Were the soldiers generally speaking relatively young men in their 20s?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not early 20s. There were older men there as well, 30 and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But anyway, as compared to other soldiers, you saw no signs that the men sent to Herzegovina were more likely to drink alcohol than anyone else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't watch them getting drunk or using drugs. I wasn't interested in that at all. That was within the purview of the security service which was in charge of that. I didn't have to monitor every single soldier, every single soldier has a platoon commander, company commander, so there were some other people who were supposed to watch their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. After Sefer Halilovic left for -- for Herzegovina, when did you next see him?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time -- or rather when I arrived at the -- Zuka's base, that was the first time I saw him down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. So is it the fact that Sefer Halilovic left on the 1st of September, before you got the order in your hand from Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, truly. However, he had already been down there before the units departed and he was down there in order to carry out preparations and to do everything else that was needed before the offensive was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, just to clinch this question, between the time when you spoke to him -- sorry, between the time when you got the order from Karavelic to go, and I mean the first order on the 3rd of September, and the time you reached Zuka's base, did you see Sefer Halilovic in that time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: From the date, the 3rd of September, when you were supposed to -- when the order said first you were supposed to leave.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I saw him once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you see him in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't. However, I think that at around that time, on the 3rd, on the 4th, I saw him but I really don't remember. We had constant contact, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Mr. Karavelic, and I, all the way up until the 3rd or the 4th. We were in almost daily contact regarding the departure of the units from Sarajevo so I saw him within that period of time but not later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, did you see him out at Hrasnica on the day you went through the tunnel, on the day you went to Bradina, you didn't see him that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, can I put to you - this - that on the night of the 7th of September, at around about 7.00, you went to Sefer Halilovic's office in Sarajevo and spoke to Sefer Halilovic there. This is -- this is just a few hours before you went through the tunnel. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th of September, the night of the 7th of September, the night of the 7th of September, the night that you went through the tunnel to Hrasnica. Did you see Sefer Halilovic at his office or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you meet Sefko Hodzic in the corridor outside his office and tell Sefko that you were going with the troops down to Jablanica? Or, sorry, I take that back, down to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is Sefko Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We might have had a problem in the translation there. We are talking about Sefko Hodzic, the journalist. Did you meet Sefko Hodzic in the corridor of Sefer Halilovic's office and tell Sefko that you were going down to Herzegovina with the troops?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefko Hodzic was known as Sefer's Friday boy and he's a journalist who reported on his behalf. I definitely didn't see him or meet him at his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we got a problem there because he says on page 63 of the 23rd of March, Your Honours, he says, on the 7th of September, "I went back to the Chief of Staff," this is at line 16, "Mr. Halilovic, at 7 in the evening and I met Celo in the corridor and I said, 'So you're going as well, Celo?' And he said 'yes.' And that's when I found out that those units were going." So you say nothing -- that that didn't happen, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not. None of that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, and of course -- well, I mean I've put that to you quite positively there. Is it your position that Sefko Hodzic is a liar?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you quite clearly what my opinion about Sefko Hodzic was. He was the first independent journalist or rather the first journalist who heard the story told by the boys. However, he did not publish anything in the media. So it is quite clear what my opinion of him is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. All right. Well let's go through the tunnel now to Hrasnica. Didn't you go through the tunnel to Hrasnica and meet there with Sefer Halilovic, on the other side of the tunnel, in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and I am sure that that didn't happen, that I didn't meet him there in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And wasn't it the case when you met him there, and Your Honours I'm referring now to page -- the transcript here at page 64 of the transcript of the 23rd of March 2005. Isn't it the fact that when you got there, you discovered that Sefer was having a lot of trouble to persuade Musan Topalovic, Caco, to go down to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, well it was because I was explaining something to the Judge. I've got to put the date of the transcript to him, so you're entitled to have that clarified. I'm putting to you on the night that we are talking about the 7th of the 9th of 1993 that you went through the tunnel, you met Sefer, and you were there told that Caco was not cooperating to go down to Herzegovina. Is that true or false?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that you, furthermore, were asked by Sefer if you could come and help persuade Caco to go, is that true or false?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when Sefer asked you to go and help persuade Caco, you said, I'm quoting at line 17, no, no, no, you don't know, Sefer, you don't know Caco. If one of his men dies, I'm going to be blamed for it and I'm going to have problems. Did you say that to Sefer?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Look, can I just put this to you? The truth is you did go down to Herzegovina with your men, all the way to Jablanica. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And this story of Konjic is just an attempt by you to move yourself away from the events at Grabovica. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be a problem even if I were in Jablanica. Had I been there I would have stated so openly because that would not -- that would not have incriminated me in any way, had I been in Jablanica, that would not have been a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave that to the Judges to decide but what I'm putting to you now is that in any event that is the fact, you did go down with the troops to Jablanica. Now, is that true or is it false?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You did in fact, you said that you went out to -- to assist -- you went out through the tunnel on Karavelic's order to assist with transportation matters. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, what did you do to resolve the transport problems?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Fikret Prevljak, if I'm not mistaken, who was a commander in Hrasnica was supposed to secure transportation for the soldiers. You probably flow yourself that the trucks could not have gone through the tunnel. So he was supposed to secure transportation for the troops and there was a problem with that because the trucks were not there. They were quite late. And then there were also problems -- there was also a problem with the food for the army. So the troops were angry. They wanted to go back through the tunnel and refused to depart to Jablanica. This is where the problems arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But what did you do about the trucks? Did you procure the trucks? Just hang on. Wait for the question to finish, please. Did you procure the trucks or were the trucks procured by Fikret Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fikret Prevljak. And some other people who were tasked with that. My job was to prevent the troops from going back to Sarajevo and to assist in order to speed up that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The truth is those trucks were procured by the president of the War Presidency at Jablanica, a man called Dr. Safet Cibo, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the truth is you were -- I'll withdraw that. In any event, it's the fact, isn't it, that you, as deputy commander of the 9th Brigade, nevertheless didn't go back through the tunnel but you set off with the troops, correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when you got to the checkpoint at Hadzici, it was you, not Senad Pecar, not Malco Rovcanin, and not any other person who took the lead in settling the dispute with the local police. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you meet Senad Pecar at Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him. I did not approach him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, your account is that when you -- when the troops got to -- down to Konjic or in the direction of Konjic, that was where you parted company with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in Bradina we parted company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you say you then went on to Konjic. What's the name of the person at whose house you stayed in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almir Habibija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you in the past give this person's name to the office of public -- sorry, the OTP in an interview as Almir Habibovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know why would I say that Habibovic or Habibi. But it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What is his real name, is it Habibija or is it Habibovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almir Habibija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Almir Dzonkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nickname of Habibija is Dzonko but not Dzonkic. So the nickname is Dzonko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we please go to private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Any way according to you the rest of your men then went along the mountain road down to Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but let me reiterate that a lot of time has passed since, but I think that they took the detour road from Bradina. They took the macadam road because the other road from Konjic to Jablanica was cut off so they had to take the detour road. At any rate, they rested in Bradina and then I continued on my own to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in what vehicle were you when you went on your own to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was it a truck or a car?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A car. A jeep or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And at that time, were you with Malco Rovcanin? You just said you were on your own. Were you with Malco Rovcanin rather than being on your own?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody was with me. I don't know if it was Rovcanin, Malco, Fikret. More likely Rovcanin, Malco but I'm not sure. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who did you say was in charge of the 9th Brigade troops who went on the mountain road to Jablanica after you departed from them?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly can't remember who it was. There were several persons that I have in mind but I can remember who exactly was the commander of that unit. It could have been a personal called Pilica. I'm not sure of his first name or last name. And then there was also somebody from the reconnaissance company. But I truly don't remember who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In reality, wasn't it Malco Rovcanin?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't believe that he could have been the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So any way there is one person whose name you can't remember who you were with when you got to Konjic. Did that person come with you to Mr. Habibija or Habibovic's house?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But he definitely didn't sleep with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, where did he sleep? Was he at Mr. Habibija's house or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but he certainly wasn't going to sleep with me and the girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. But you see you're making a claim that you were somewhere else and I'm asking you about who you were with and who can verify this -- this account of yours. So the question remains -- well you say you can't remember where this person slept. Can I ask you did they come to Habibija's house at all or Habibovic's house at all?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask Mr. Malco whether he went or not. I'm sure that he will tell you. You could also ask Habibija, Almir and his wife. They are definitely going to tell you that. It's for you to verify all these things. That's your job. I'm telling you things and you can verify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, I'm going to ask you the questions about what you say and later on we'll have a look at the Malco situation. Any way, what you say is that you went to this house. Did you procure any weapons there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a house, it's an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Anyway, did you procure any weapons there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What did you procure there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't remember, but on several occasions, we went to Mr. Almir Habibija to collect weapons gathered by him down there in that area, but I don't remember what we took on that occasion. I know that we took some weaponry but I don't recall exactly what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you have communications equipment with you in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I don't know but I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was Adnan Solakovic with you in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, look, you were with one person -- one other person you've indicated to us and I want to know who that was, Mr. Delalic. You know who Adnan Solakovic is, commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion, correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what I'm asking you now is was Adnan Solakovic, commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion, with you in Konjic? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember. I don't know. It's possible that he was there but I really don't know. I cannot be certain of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And who were you with on the way down to -- sorry, I'm just noticing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you're finished with Konjic, we will have a break, yes. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, just before the witness comes in, there are a couple of management matters that I just wanted to raise. The first one concerns some things that are going to happen in Prosecution -- in cross-examination now and I just thought I better raise them with the Court before we start. The first is that, as you have seen, I've been confronting the witness with certain statements of other witnesses and we now come to Jablanica. And here I need to confront him with the statements of some of his own 9th Brigade people, including witness D, and perhaps if we could go -- I think we need to go into private session even for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So that's -- that's coming. And the final matter simply concerns the 1996 statement to which this witness has referred. We are obviously very concerned to get the tape that he's referred to, if it's true, and I just ask you what the progress about that is at this stage, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been discussing this matter with counsel. Prosecution has made inquiries or, let's say, are in the process of making inquiries. I've been trying to get hold of the old investigators, if indeed it's true that there was such a statement. I have managed to get hold of one investigator who was working on this case. Your Honour, by way of explanation this is before the Nikolai time so there were two other investigators who have been working and who did occasion to see Mr. Delalic. I have got hold of one of them and I've actually telephoned him or rather my assistant has telephoned him and he -- his answer to us is he does not recall whether a statement was taken. There is another investigator whose telephone number I've just obtained this morning because it's difficult to track him down and I will be also making inquiries from him during the next break, Your Honour. I will try and call him and see if I can get hold of him. So we do not have a 96 statement in house. That's the bottom line. And I'm trying to inquire from them if one was indeed taken, and this is because counsel have asked and perhaps further clarification from this witness in cross-examination will reveal what was the nature of this and who he gave it to, although he doesn't recall the name but it could only have been one of these two investigators. So we are trying our hardest, Your Honour, in respect to this 96 but there is nothing that our searches have thrown up. And yesterday we did run more searches in respect of many issues just to make quite sure that we go over with a fine-tooth comb. So we have with all due diligence tried as hard as we can to come up with the information and these are matters beyond our control, Your Honour, because these are people who have since left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think I believe Mr. Morrissey is competent to get more information about that interview from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just indicate that we certainly accept that Ms. Chana personally is doing all that she can reasonably do at this stage and we are grateful for that. I have to say we might make a comment about the Prosecution as an institution at a later time but we are very convinced of the good faith of the inquiries that are happening right now. We want that to be put on record at his stage. Your Honours, those are the only matters I want to raise right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, can you finish this witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I hope so and I'm trying to. It depends. Yesterday he was answering very shortly. Today there has been a change but I suspect that the answer is yes and it's realistic to plan on the basis yes and that's what we are aiming for, but I can indicate that we'll comfortably go into tomorrow and it really depends how he answers some questions here. However, we should plan on the basis that we'll finish him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. How about the next witness on Monday? Do you have any proofing notes or whether he was arrived in The Hague or how soon you could provide those information to Defence and the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour the next witness has been taken by David Re. He's not due here in The Hague until Saturday afternoon so Mr. Re will be proofing him on Sunday and hopefully the proofing notes will be provided by Sunday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the next week we are sitting in the morning and the time is really too short for that. I hope that at least one day before his testimony, he should arrive in The Hague. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are some genuine problems about that. There are some witnesses we can jump quickly which we did with the pathologist and so on. This witness is one who, depending on what he says, might be quite a lengthy witness and might take some document -- there might be some document warfare that occurs with him and he's a witness who provided a very -- it's a six page statement, I think in substance. It's about confined issues, I have to say. I notice that with the withdrawal of Mr. Mujezinovic, it may well be that the Prosecution aren't persisting with a particular line they are taking and it might -- and it depends because the statement itself is brief, so I need to know in a sense what line the Prosecution are taking with Mr. -- with that witness and depending upon that, things might proceed sensibly. But I have to point out that at the moment the Prosecution are alleging that they have to call an expert. Your Honours haven't ruled upon that as yet. But it seems to me not feasible to deal with the expert at short notice and also that witness at short notice. We think it's -- not feasible to deal with the expert at short notice at all in any event but we are being put in a position now where Mr. Halilovic won't be properly -- won't have justice done in effect by me. I'll be unprepared because these witnesses are both certainly the expert and possibly the other witness are at the moment unknown quantities to some degree. So that does pose a problem us. We don't want to delay things. It's not in anyone's interest to delay, and I'm -- we can all think about sensible alternatives but I don't like the option of getting the proofing notes the evening of the day before that particular witness arrives. I can say that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. We will take into account your submissions. Well, could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Delalic. Mr. Delalic were you interviewed by the Prosecutors in November of last year, whilst you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And was that interview among the people present at that interview, was the learned Prosecutor, Ms. Chana, present?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And was it -- was that interview taped on a tape recorder, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment. Okay. Now, on that occasion, at tape number 3107/1, side A, at page 33 of 53, you say this: "So basically we arrived in Konjic in very, very early morning hours and I stopped by and took some rest for several hours maybe." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. I think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you then say, "So I slept in the apartment of this Almir Habibovic"?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And why was it that you gave his name as Habibovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was perhaps a mistake because the majority of the names of our names end in an "ic," but I think this is really a mistake. Perhaps I made a mistake but his name is actually Almir Habibija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Your Honours could we please go into the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to put -- I just want to put some evidence to you. I'm going to put some evidence to you now that's been given in this Court. This is on the 17th of February, page 40, Your Honours. I mention 17th of February, Witness, because that's when the evidence was given here, but we are not asking about that date. We are asking about the time when these troops went down to Jablanica and Grabovica. All right. I'm going to put questions and answers from the witness: Question: "When you got to Zuka's base, did you see Celo, Ramiz Delalic? Did he get out of the truck buses?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "And what did he do?" Answer: "He went inside. I don't know who he talked to but he was looking for accommodation for us because the first thing for anyone to secure was food and accommodation, and he was taking care of his men." Now, Mr. Delalic, that evidence that I've just read out to you, that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me go on further. And now I'm recommencing where we stopped at line 16: Question: "Did he inform you as the men of the results of his inquiries of accommodation?" Answer: "We were only told later that we were going to Grabovica." Question: "When you say later, do you mean before you set off for Grabovica?" Answer: "Yes. After that conversation he had, when he came back, when Celo came back, we were told that we were going to Grabovica." Now, Mr. Delalic, once again, the evidence that you've just heard read out to you, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll move to another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is evidence given on the 22nd of February at page 60 of the transcript. No, no. No, just excuse me a moment, please. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, while Mr. Morrissey is looking for his papers, I'm not sure whether the witness is aware as to what's being put to him. I think because we already talked about it before, we all are very aware, perhaps it would be good to make the witness aware that this is evidence which has been given in this court by witnesses, the protection, so he understands, because I -- he may be aware.
